name: Boyd Acres
label: Boyd Acres
about_prose: Boyd Acres sits in the northeastern corner of Bend, bounded by Hamby Road to the east, the Deschutes River to the west, Mt. Washington Drive, the North Unit Canal, and Butler Market Road to the south, and Cooley Road to the north. It straddles both US-97 and US-20, so most streets reach the Bend Parkway within a few turns, and the big-box retail at Cascade Village sits inside the neighborhood's southern edge. It is one of Bend's larger neighborhood-association districts by area.

The neighborhood is named for Charles William Boyd, a rancher who arrived in Central Oregon in 1904 and built a cattle operation that grew to around 600 acres at its peak. His ranch buildings were moved a short distance in the late 1970s to a site just north of the Bend River Promenade, where they still stand today as the Pomegranate Home and Garden shop. A working ranch structure from before Bend's development boom, still standing under a new use instead of demolished for one, is unusual in a neighborhood built mostly in the past two decades.

Three irrigation canals, the Swalley, the North Unit, and the Pilot Butte, split off the Deschutes River just outside Boyd Acres and cross the neighborhood on their way to farms further out. They are working infrastructure, not a decorative water feature. Dug mostly by pickaxe and shovel more than a century ago, they still move water today. A 1.5-mile stretch of the Pilot Butte Canal between Cooley Road and Yeoman Road was added to the National Register of Historic Places in February 2016, recognized for its role in the canal-fed irrigation that helped settle Central Oregon starting in 1903.

Most homes were built after 2000, a mix of Craftsman, Northwest Contemporary, and Ranch styles on lots that range from under a tenth of an acre to nearly 20 acres. Pockets of houses from the 1970s and 1980s remain scattered through the older sections, so a buyer touring Boyd Acres sees a genuine range of building eras on the same streets rather than one subdivision's single build-out.

The Boyd Acres Neighborhood Association is one of 13 city-recognized neighborhood associations in Bend. It is not a homeowners association. It carries no design covenants and no dues of its own, and it exists to give residents a direct channel to Bend's city council rather than to enforce a rulebook. Its recent advocacy has focused on Empire Avenue, covering pedestrian and bike routes, Cascades East Transit access, and roundabouts at key intersections, the kind of fight a resident joins by showing up to a meeting, not by paying an assessment.

The park system is deep for one neighborhood. Pine Nursery Park, 159 acres on NE Purcell Boulevard, holds 16 pickleball courts, four softball fields, a 14-acre off-leash dog area, and an ODFW-stocked fishing pond. Rockridge Park, 36.6 acres beside Lava Ridge Elementary and Sky View Middle School, adds an 11,000-square-foot skatepark, a nine-hole disc golf course, and more than a mile of bike skills trails, built around old-growth juniper and lava rock rather than cleared for it. Boyd Park, three acres on Comet Lane, is the smaller option, with a playground, a picnic pavilion, and soft-surface trails within walking distance for streets that aren't near the two larger parks. Kids in the neighborhood attend Lava Ridge Elementary and, in the Bend-La Pine district, Mountain View High School, which enrolled about 1,261 students in the 2023-2024 school year.

An industrial quarter bounded by Empire Avenue, Boyd Acres Road, Brinson Boulevard, and NE 18th Street has become Bend's production-brewery district. Bridge 99, Boneyard, Crux Fermentation Project, North Rim, Oblivion, and 10 Barrel all operate facilities there, drawn by industrial zoning, an enterprise-zone tax designation, and direct access to US-97. That district sits inside Boyd Acres' own boundary, not screened off in a separate business park across town.

Boyd Acres suits buyers who want newer construction, larger lots than central Bend typically offers, and quick highway access over a walk-everywhere layout close to downtown. It won't suit buyers chasing the tree-lined, older-growth feel of Bend's original neighborhoods, since most of this land was still ranch and canal frontage within living memory. The honest trade-off is structural, not cosmetic. Two highways cut through the middle of the neighborhood, and the streets nearest the interchanges carry the traffic and noise that come with that access.

amenities.name: Pine Nursery Park
amenities.description: A 159-acre Bend Park and Recreation park at 3750 NE Purcell Blvd with 16 pickleball courts (8 lighted), four softball fields, a 14-acre off-leash dog area, an ODFW-stocked fishing pond, disc golf, and an all-abilities playground.

amenities.name: Rockridge Park
amenities.description: A 36.6-acre park at 20885 Egypt Drive with an 11,000-square-foot skatepark, a 9-hole disc golf course, over a mile of bike skills trails, and two playgrounds, preserving old-growth juniper and lava rock.
amenities.access: Open 5 AM to 10 PM; beside Lava Ridge Elementary and Sky View Middle

amenities.name: Boyd Park
amenities.description: A 3-acre neighborhood park at 20750 Comet Lane with a multi-age playground, picnic pavilion, basketball half-court, and soft-surface trails with mountain views.

amenities.name: Lava Ridge Elementary
amenities.description: A Bend-La Pine Schools K-5 at 20805 Cooley Road within the Boyd Acres attendance zone.

amenities.name: Mountain View High School
amenities.description: The public high school serving Boyd Acres, at 2755 NE 27th Street, with about 1,261 students in grades 9-12.

amenities.name: Pilot Butte Canal Historic Segment
amenities.description: A 1.5-mile segment of the 1903 Pilot Butte Canal between Cooley and Yeoman Roads, added to the National Register of Historic Places in February 2016.
